## Introduction

In this document, I aimed to pool the distance data (of clusters) from the three time periods (2000, 2007, 2015) to estimate the abundance of Black-eared Miner clusters and individuals. The purpose of pooling the data was to increase the sample size and increase precision of abundance estimates.

## Load packages and data

```{r}
#| warning: false
library(Distance)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# read data
data.2015 <- read.csv("Data/data.frame.2015b.csv", header = TRUE)
data.2007 <- read.csv("Data/data.frame.2007.csv", header = TRUE)
data.2000 <- read.csv("Data/data.frame.2000e.csv", header = TRUE)

# prepare data
data.2000 <- data.2000 %>%
  mutate(Region.Label = 
           case_when(Region.Label == "Bookmark" ~ as.factor(2000)))
data.2007 <- data.2007 %>%
  mutate(Region.Label = 
           case_when(Region.Label == "Bookmark" ~ as.factor(2007)) )
data.2015 <- data.frame(Region.Label = rep(as.factor(2015), nrow(data.2015)), 
                        Area = data.2015$Area, 
                        Sample.Label = data.2015$Sample.Label,
                        Effort = data.2015$Effort,
                        distance = data.2015$distance,
                        size = data.2015$size)

data.pooled <- rbind(data.2000, data.2015) # left out 2007 because of inconsistent sampling of only unburnt areas

data.pooled <- data.pooled %>%
  mutate(size = if_else(size < 6, NA_real_, as.numeric(size)),
         distance = if_else(is.na(size), NA_real_, as.numeric(distance)),
         Area = 900)

nrow(data.pooled[!is.na(data.pooled$distance),]) # how many datapoints
```

I only use the data from 2000 and 2015 because the sampling protocols are similar (i.e., entire 900 sq km sampled, instead of only unburnt areas sampled in 2017). I also ignore geographical stratification (i.e., OLD vs. BURNT) because `ds()` cannot accomodate changes in stratification between time periods (i.e., `Area` has to be consistent within each strata).

Instead, I treat `Year` as the stratification factor to allow year-specific estimates of abundance later on. Assumptions associated with this decision are: (i)

## Distance analysis

I select a binning interval of 20m, with right-truncation at 100m to avoid non-monotonicity in the detection fit...

I first fit a model with year treated as a stratification factor (i.e., under `Region.Label`). By combining years, detection functions fitted for all years are the same key function, but the scale parameter of the key function differs between years.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
conversion <- convert_units("meter", "meter", "square kilometer")
mybreaks <- seq(0,100,20) 

# half-normal
hn_strat <- ds(data.pooled, 
                truncation = list(left=0, right=100), 
              convert_units = conversion, cutpoints = mybreaks,
              key = "hn", adjustment = "cos", #order = 2, 
              formula=~as.factor(Region.Label))

# check fit
plot(hn_strat, main="", xlab="Distance (m)",
     showpoints=FALSE, lwd=3, xlim=c(0, 100),pdf=F) 
```

Examining the `summary()` output, we see the year-specific estimates being provided:

```{r}
#| warning: false
summary(hn_strat)
```

The summary also shows beta parameters associated with year-specific estimates of the shape parameter of the half-normal key function. The standard errors of the beta (for 2015) is larger than the estimate itself. This suggests there us not a strong 'year' signal on the shape of the detection functions. Perhaps a model with a pooled detection function would be equally suitable for these data. See reference [here](https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/O3K16BPXx-Q/m/KqzAG8upCAAJ).

```{r}
hn_pooled <- ds(data.pooled, 
                truncation = list(left=0, right=100), 
              convert_units = conversion, cutpoints = mybreaks,
              key = "hn", adjustment = "cos")
```

Having a look at the point and interval estimates of the two models bears out the minute difference between the models.

```{r}
dens_yrcov <- hn_strat$dht$individuals$D
dens_cons <- hn_pooled$dht$individuals$D

compare_est <- rbind( data.frame(year = dens_yrcov$Label,
                           estimate = dens_yrcov$Estimate,
                           lcl = dens_yrcov$lcl,
                           ucl = dens_yrcov$ucl,
                           Method = "Year cov."),
                      data.frame(year = dens_cons$Label,
                           estimate = dens_cons$Estimate,
                           lcl = dens_cons$lcl,
                           ucl = dens_cons$ucl,
                           Method = "Pooled") )

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(compare_est, aes(x=year, y=estimate, shape = Method)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lcl, ymax=ucl), color="black", 
                  position=position_dodge(width=0.3)) +
  labs(x="Year", y = "Miners per sq km")
```

We can go with the pooled model, which has a slightly smaller year-specific CV($\hat{D}$); i.e., higher precision.

Comparing the 2015 density estimates with that of the previous document ("1_Nest-vs-First.pdf"), we see lower point estimates (6.18 vs 7.16) and an improvement in precision (CV = 0.20 vs 0.25). The lower density estimate is likely a ???

The improvement in CV likely comes from the better detection model fit to the data (with a truncation distance of 100m and binning distance of 20m) AND some pooling effect.
